The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • It has been revealed that A customer writes in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

It has been revealed that A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

According to recent reports, the AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

Industry observers note that an AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

According to recent reports, that gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

Recent findings suggest that you can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

According to recent reports, final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

In a recent development, A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

According to recent reports, an agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

In a recent development, we use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Industry observers note that table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

According to recent reports, one good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

It has been revealed that figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

According to recent reports, kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Industry observers note that kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Sources indicate that capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

In a recent development, we took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

According to recent reports, this is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

It has been revealed that figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

Industry observers note that the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Recent findings suggest that now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

Sources indicate that none of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

Recent findings suggest that what to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Industry observers note that classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

According to recent reports, every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

Sources indicate that at the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

It has been revealed that the trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

Recent findings suggest that thinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

In a recent development, gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

Sources indicate that now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:.

Breaking: Introducing ambient networking for GKE

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Network sidecars have a deserved reputation for excessive resource consumption  and increased management overhead, especially in a service mesh environment.
  • The ambient networking architecture shifts networking responsibilities from individual application pods to shared per-node components and managed control plane services.
  • The ambient networking control plane orchestrates operations across the cluster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Network sidecars have a deserved reputation for excessive resource consumption  and increased management overhead, especially in a service mesh environment. Today, we are announcing the general availability of ambient networking for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). This milestone marks an important evolution in how your run service mesh on GKE, bringing a sidecar-less architecture into production. Introduced earlier this year, ambient networking decouples functionality traditionally provided as a service mesh from application workloads, allowing platform operators and developers to help secure, observe, and route traffic without the resource overhead and operational complexity of managing sidecar proxies.

The ambient networking architecture shifts networking responsibilities from individual application pods to shared per-node components and managed control plane services.

The ambient networking control plane orchestrates operations across the cluster.

At the same time, several Node-level management components operate securely within the gke-managed-ambient namespace:.

Ambient networking runtime interface (NRI) plugin: Integrates with the NRI to perform low-level network redirection, intercepting traffic to and from ambient-enabled application pods.

xDS agent (ambient agent): Runs inside the node proxy pod to receive xDS configuration updates from Traffic Director and request certificates from the GKE control plane on-demand.

Node proxy (L4 Envoy proxy): A high-performance, shared per-node Envoy instance that processes intercepted L4 traffic, enforces mutual TLS (mTLS), evaluates authorization policies, performs load balancing, and emits rich telemetry metrics.

Service pods: The user’s application/service pods communicate through the GKE node proxy to perform service to service mTLS across the cluster.

Together, these features combine to deliver a number of advanced capabilities for GKE environments:.

Sources indicate that zero Trust architecture: Ambient networking allows customers to establish a Zero Trust security posture. Traffic between workloads can be automatically encrypted using mutual TLS (mTLS) with managed workload identities, helping protect and secure service-to-service communication across the cluster.

Ambient networking delivers tangible value for GKE operators:.

Simpler operations: Traditionally, service mesh products rely on injecting sidecar containers directly into every workload pod. Ambient networking removes this sidecar dependency by shifting networking features to shared node components. This fully managed solution simplifies deployment and streamlines day-to-day cluster operations.

Simplified lifecycle management: When proxy logic is decoupled from application containers, lifecycle management is simplified. Upgrading proxy versions or applying configuration updates helps avoid restarting application workloads or scheduling downtime windows, enabling continuous availability for your services. Ambient networking can reduce administrative overhead and application disruption an average of four times annually by eliminating pod restarts required by CVE patches for L4 mesh usage.This fully managed solution can be installed either at cluster creation time or added to an existing cluster. Ongoing maintenance to the cluster components is handled by automated systems and is performed along with normal GKE cluster maintenance.

Simplifying adoption by removing the cost and complexity barriers of sidecars. Try it out in your GKE environment and experience the benefits of ambient networking:.

fully managed installation and upgrades.

service-to-service mTLS and authorization policies.

lower resource usage than sidecars.

See our documentation for more information: https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ambient-overview.

Pricing: https://cloud.google.com/products/gke-service-networking/pricing.

When Figures Disagree with Text: Evaluating Autonomous Visual Evidence Verification in Scientific Papers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (304 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.24353v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Scientific figures carry evidence for the claims that cite them, so reviewing a paper means checking that a figure agrees with the text, and not only describing what the figure demonstrates. Benchmarks of figure-text verification typically hand the model the figure, the claim, or the knowledge that an inconsistency exists, which leaves untested whether a model can find the figure worth checking in a complete paper, relate a visual element to the claim it conflicts with, and recognize the conflict. We study this autonomous setting on 31 full manuscripts, each carrying a reviewer-documented figure-text inconsistency from PRISMM-Bench that is hidden from the model. Six multimodal models review each PDF under a neutral prompt, and we then add one input at a time to the same manuscripts. Of 1,445 open-ended reviews, 60.6% mention the flawed figure, yet a grading rubric accepts only 3.3% as diagnosing its contradiction; a blind audit finds the rubric lenient, so we read these as rubric-accepted rates and compare conditions rather than absolute values. In a separate controlled run, naming the figure, without stating that it is flawed, raises rubric-accepted diagnosis from 4.3% to 20.4%, while a consistency instruction and coarse visual cues do not. When the contradiction is visible only in the rendered figure, text-only review yields no accepted diagnosis, while review of the rendered pages with the figure named reaches 15.8%. A baseline that lets the model choose which figures to check, ranked by centrality, stays at 4.8%. Deciding what to verify is thus a large part of the difficulty, and the selection rule we tested does not resolve it. Multimodal document understanding should be evaluated on whether a model can propose what to verify, not only answer questions about a figure it is handed.

Breaking: Introducing the Apache Spark Optimization Agent for AWS Glue ETL

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AWS Glue ETL now offers the Apache Spark Optimization Agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations within minutes.
  • The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen goal and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Apache Spark Optimization Agent is available at no additional charge for AWS Glue versions 4.0 and later in all Regions where AWS Glue is available, except the AWS GovCloud (US) and China Regions.

According to recent reports, AWS Glue ETL now offers the Apache Spark Optimization Agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations within minutes. You can select a cost or performance goal, and the agent returns specific configuration changes with the telemetry evidence and reasoning behind each suggestion. You can use the agent on any completed job run from the AWS Glue console, or from your own tools through the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio MCP Server.

The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen goal and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine. The engine reads all job artifacts together to identify what is driving runtime and cost: too little parallelism, a skewed join key, memory pressure forcing spill, idle executors, or capacity provisioned beyond what the job uses. When cost and performance trade off, the agent improves the metric you chose while keeping any regression of the other within defined limits. The engine also checks best practices such as platform-level improvements like upgrading to a newer AWS Glue version or using AWS Graviton processors. Each recommendation is labeled by the area it modifies: infrastructure, Spark configuration, code, or data layout. All access is authenticated with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and logged in AWS CloudTrail.

Recent findings suggest that the Apache Spark Optimization Agent is available at no additional charge for AWS Glue versions 4.0 and later in all Regions where AWS Glue is available, except the AWS GovCloud (US) and China Regions. To get started, see Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR and AWS Glue and the blog post - Introducing the Apache Spark optimization agent for Amazon EMR Serverless and AWS Glue ETL.

Introducing Falcon ASR

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1249 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.
  • Sources indicate that we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect.
  • Sources indicate that in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

Sources indicate that we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

Sources indicate that in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

In a recent development, the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

Sources indicate that WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

It has been revealed that we evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

In a recent development, public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

According to recent reports, falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

Industry observers note that we included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

Sources indicate that نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

Recent findings suggest that درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

Industry observers note that WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

In a recent development, تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:.

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

Recent findings suggest that ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

In a recent development, نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

يعكيكم العافية علي المجهود الطيب... بس بغينا نشوف موديلات صوتية STSو TTS بالللهجة الإماراتية لو أمكن.

How Vodafone is using the Data Engineering Agent to improve their data pipelines

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manager, Data & Analytics Engineering, Vodafone.
  • Industry observers note that for large organizations, building and maintaining data pipelines is one of the most complex tasks that data engineering teams are tasked with.
  • In this blog post, Vodafone Czech Republic describes how it has used the Data Engineering Agent to modernize and optimize BigQuery stored procedures, transforming them into modern data pipelines and reducing pipeline execution times by half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sr. Manager, Data & Analytics Engineering, Vodafone.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Industry observers note that for large organizations, building and maintaining data pipelines is one of the most complex tasks that data engineering teams are tasked with. In BigQuery environments, the Data Engineering Agent can help, leveraging Gemini to to automate these workflows.

In this blog post, Vodafone Czech Republic describes how it has used the Data Engineering Agent to modernize and optimize BigQuery stored procedures, transforming them into modern data pipelines and reducing pipeline execution times by half. - Pedro Esteves, Google Cloud.

The Data Engineering Agent makes it easy to build and maintain modern data pipelines. The agent is available in BigQuery pipelines and Dataform. At Vodafone, we used the agent directly in Dataform to build Dataform pipelines. As shown in the example below, the Data Engineering Agent takes natural language instructions together with any code provided in the instruction file to build the Dataform pipeline.

Industry observers note that vodafone Czech Republic uses many BigQuery stored procedures to transform data for business purposes. These stored procedures are a legacy of a previous on-premises data warehouse migration to BigQuery. Many of them contain 2,000 or 3,000 lines of code and run sequentially.

Compared to a modular Dataform approach created by the Data Engineering Agent, there are several known disadvantages of maintaining legacy, multi-thousand-line stored procedures, as described in the table below.

Legacy stored procedures (Monolith).

Single file, 1000s of lines, complex logic mixed.

Copy/Paste code blocks (prone to drift).

functions and ref() for strict logic reuse.

Automated testing (Unique, Not Null, Referential Integrity) built-in.

Comments in code (usually outdated).

Auto-generated documentation with lineage graph.

Manual scheduling; hard-coded dependency management.

Automatic execution based on lineage (DAG).

To solve the problems of running and maintaining legacy stored procedures, we used the Data Engineering Agent to migrate some of the stored procedures into Dataform pipelines.

The Data Engineering Agent was able to parallelize the code into independent steps which are then run in parallel to improve readability and performance. See the example below:.

The Data Engineering Agent can understand dependencies between the tables and cache certain intermediate tables using BigQuery materialized views. This means that tables that are used in downstream processes can be cached, speeding up code execution and reducing cost.

Having a modular pipeline allows us to facilitate end-to-end orchestration and pipeline dependencies to meet our SLAs. Before using Dataform, we had to manually control pipeline execution by creating metadata tables with several checkpoints and logs. Dependencies between stored procedures jobs were also maintained manually in a spreadsheet. By executing the pipeline in Dataform, all the dependencies and execution logs are handled by Dataform.

Because the code is now split into several steps, it’s possible to execute only a subset of the actions in Dataform rather than running the entire stored procedure. This can help with debugging and gives us the flexibility to only run the relevant sections of the code.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a trade-off between parallelization and caching. When we prompted the Data Engineering Agent to parallelize our procedures, we noticed an increase in cost.

When running a standard sequential stored procedure, BigQuery caches the base table for the first thread. However, splitting this logic into parallel streams can inadvertently negate those caching benefits, causing full table scans for each thread.

To solve this, we asked the Data Engineering Agent to create materialized views for intermediate tables. These views effectively pre-cache the data, ensuring that your parallelized queries remain performant and cost-efficient.

To make the agent parallelize the code more efficiently we gave it specific instructions on which areas (staging tables) we were interested in parallelizing.

Deploying Data Engineering Agent delivered immediate and measurable impact, specifically in addressing the toil associated with legacy migrations. The agent successfully achieved high-fidelity replication of all stored procedures, ensuring 1:1 logic parity with minimal human intervention.

In a recent development, by automating the conversion of complex ETL pipelines, the agent achieved a 90% reduction in migration time compared with traditional manual approaches. What would have typically required weeks of engineering effort was completed in a fraction of the time, freeing engineers to focus on other key tasks.

According to recent reports, furthermore, the modernization of the underlying infrastructure resulted in substantial performance gains. Post-migration benchmarks indicate that the fresh data pipelines run twice as fast, significantly reducing query latency and increasing overall data throughput.

And as we previously discussed, instructing the agent to cache intermediate tables led to a 30% reduction in costs.

Industry observers note that beyond accelerating development and reducing costs, these agentic tools are also changing the way data engineers approach their work. Rather than spending significant time on repetitive migration and optimization tasks, engineers can collaborate with agents to explore different implementation options, validate design decisions, and accelerate delivery. This shift is encouraging teams to adopt latest ways of working, where agentic capabilities become an integral part of the development process and help shape how data solutions are designed, delivered, and maintained.

At Vodafone, we’re planning to scale the use of the Data Engineering Agent across the organization in the following key areas:.

Standardized Dataform template repository: Establishing a central repository for Dataform templates allows for consistent architecture and design patterns across different projects and teams, helping ensure quality and alignment with global standards.

Global market onboarding: We will expand the Data Engineering Agent deployment across key Vodafone markets including the Czech Republic (CZ), Romania (RO), Ireland (IE), Germany (DE), and the United Kingdom (UK), to drive widespread adoption and modernization.

Integration with developer environments (IDEs): Deepening the integration of agentic capabilities directly into developer workflows (such as VS Code, and and Antigravity) will enable engineers to leverage Data Engineering Agent features within their existing tools and IDEs.

Federated CI/CD governance: Implementing a centralized yet flexible governance framework for Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) will allow individual markets to maintain autonomy while adhering to corporate quality and security policies.

Modernization of legacy stored procedures at scale: By systematically migrating complex, legacy workloads — specifically SAS code, BTEQ scripts, and MicroStrategy — into modern Dataform pipelines will allow us to reduce technical debt and accelerate transformation across the enterprise.

Industry observers note that to learn more about transforming your enterprise data architecture for the agentic era, download our complete Data Agents Guidebook or explore Google Cloud’s Rapid Migration and Modernization Program (RaMP). To get started building and optimizing your own data pipelines with the agent today, visit the Data Engineering Agent pipelines documentation.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.24347v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: The search for better models, whether expressed as analytical equations or neural architectures, has increasingly shifted from manual design toward data-driven automation. While a multitude of algorithms exist, ranging from exhaustive search to AlphaEvolve, recent advances in general-purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex raise the question: could providing such systems with a "model discovery recipe" be enough to discover or improve models? We present automodel, an agent skill for general model discovery. With case studies in astrophysics, cardiovascular dynamics, precision agriculture, traffic flow, and vehicle tire dynamics, we show how commercial agents equipped with automodel can successfully identify novel and scientifically-relevant models. Our findings suggest that encoding model-discovery methodology as a portable agent skill can provide a simple, interactive, powerful and broadly applicable alternative to domain-specific automated discovery pipelines. The skill is available at: https://github.com/unlayer-ai/automodel.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (218 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.24324v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: AI coding agents have become one of the most popular applications of large language models. Yet, agentic AI comes at the cost of a tremendous amount of GPU compute resources, which limits its profitability and its viability at scale. In this paper, we investigate whether smaller, cheaper models can cut this cost without sacrificing accuracy. We evaluate 36 popular large and small open-weight models released since 2024 on a software engineering benchmark, and find that recent small models are closing the accuracy gap compared to their large counterparts. We investigate the structure of this gap and find that the gap is highly concentrated around hard tasks that small language models fail to solve while achieving remarkably good accuracy for easy and medium complexity tasks. Following this observation, we show that by utilizing a hybrid inference strategy that tries a small model first and escalates to a large one only when needed, we can achieve up to 33% reduction in total GPU-hour costs and 16.4% on all tasks from SWE-bench Verified, without sacrificing accuracy. Strikingly, this simple cascade nearly matches an oracle-style task router, highlighting a practical path for deploying cost-aware coding agents in production without complex learned task routers and with minimal engineering complexity.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.24321v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Scientific problems have no answer key, so evaluating an agent means deciding what counts as a better solution before any agent is run. Existing benchmarks either match a symbolic answer against a key or, where they require executable work, score it by unit tests, by a rubric, or by position on a competition leaderboard. None of these is the criterion by which a field decides that one published method beats another. STEMBench adopts that criterion directly. Each of its twelve research problems in high-energy physics, astrophysics and neuroscience is scored by its own field's figure of merit, and each comes with two measured anchors: a submission that uses no domain knowledge, and an expert reference reproducing a published method, both obtained by running code shipped with the benchmark. The interval between them states how much of a problem is crossed by scientific insight rather than by engineering. Across eight frontier models, task-level wins and domain-level leadership dissociate: a model that wins five of the twelve tasks leads no domain mean. In the high-effort cross-model comparison, at least one model's mean score exceeds the expert anchor on seven of twelve tasks. The remaining five span uncertainty estimation, latent and causal inference, and cross-site clinical classification. Numerical scores and official-submission validity capture different aspects of performance and are reported separately. We release the tasks, graders, anchors and harness.

Director, Engineering, Google Ads.

Group Product Manager, Data Cloud.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Ever wonder how the Google Ads team keeps the massive system stable and online, despite continuous attempts by hackers to take it down? Part of the answer is using Spanner as its core operational and graph database.

In a recent development, the Google Ads team uses a central graph-based platform to fight fraud and abuse with batch and real-time signals. Built to protect the Google Ads ecosystem and now used by multiple teams across Google, the platform organizes anti-abuse intelligence into a single, interconnected view. Its core mission is simple but critical: uncover hidden connections between malicious assets in real time before they can harm owners or advertisers. This blog talks about the challenging modern fraud and abuse landscape, and how Spanner, specifically Spanner Graph, helps Google successfully detect those threats.

The need for a graph-based abuse detection platform stems from how the global threat landscape has evolved. Digital advertising fraud and online scams are no longer minor operational nuisances, they are a massive drain on the global economy. According to the NASDAQ Global Financial Crime Report, total global fraud losses are estimated at nearly $580 billion for 2025. Furthermore, global surveys indicate that approximately one in five adults fall victim to scams. In digital ads, fraud and abuse waste marketing spend, corrupt attribution data, and expose everyday customers to financial scams, identity theft, and malware.

Bad actors are increasingly leveraging automation and AI to scale deceptive campaigns more efficiently. In 2025 alone, Google blocked or removed more than 8.3 billion policy-violating ads and suspended 24.9 million advertiser accounts. As these tactics evolve, real-time detection becomes more key for protecting businesses and owners.

Defending applications from fraud and abuse requires continuously advancing threat detection beyond traditional, point-in-time checks. To do that, modern security systems must address two compounding challenges simultaneously:.

Fraud and abuse operate as networks: Bad actors hide behind residential proxies and synthetic identities to create deceptive ad campaigns. Each of the attributes like location proxies, account, and identity parameters  appear benign in isolation. But behind the scenes, bad actors share payment methods, domains, and accounts, requiring security systems to target entire coordinated clusters of fraud rather than isolated indicators. This is hard to capture with traditional approaches that do not understand the relationship between attributes and evaluates each signal separately.

In a recent development, detection must scale dynamically: As the graph-based abuse detection platform grew, the previous system, based on offline MapReduce batch processing, became bottlenecked. Tracing multi-hop relationships in batch MapReduce required repeated, expensive joins across distributed stages, triggering massive intermediate data expansions, heavy shuffle overhead, and network bottlenecks that caused hours-long latencies and combinatorial fanouts during multi-hop traversals.

In critical scenarios like halting live malware campaigns, multi-hour latency gaps leave room for a lot of damage. To block sophisticated fraud rings, Google needed to evaluate multi-hop relationship risks in real time at the time of serving these ads, before malicious content reaches users.

To overcome the limits of processing at inference time, the engineering team needed a database that could ingest live signals from a large number of sources via pub/sub streams, all while delivering horizontal elasticity, global transactional consistency, and sub-second multi-hop traversals. The solution was to modernize Google's graph-based abuse detection platform for Ads onto Spanner Graph.

According to recent reports, because Ads’ core transactional and entity data already lived in Spanner, they didn’t need to migrate any data in order to adopt Spanner Graph. Rather than standing up a separate, specialized graph database, the team simply defined property graphs directly on top of their existing relational tables.

This delivered several benefits:.

In a recent development, from hour-long batch jobs to sub-second queries: Spanner Graph co-locates graph traversal computations directly with the underlying distributed data splits to minimize join overhead. Multi-hop traversals that previously took an hour in offline Apache Flume MapReduce jobs now execute on live production data with sub-second to single-digit millisecond latency.

Zero-ETL adoption in weeks, not months: Because there was no data to move, most graph-based abuse detection use cases transitioned to Spanner Graph within weeks. Layering a graph directly onto existing Spanner tables eliminated fragile synchronization pipelines and redundant storage costs.

Expressive pattern matching with native ISO GQL: Instead of writing and maintaining complex custom traversal code, engineers now query the exact same tables using standard ISO Graph Query Language (GQL), significantly accelerating feature velocity.

In a recent development, with Spanner Graph, Google's graph-based abuse detection platform for ads performs multi-hop pattern matching directly against operational relational data using ISO GQL. For instance, when an account is flagged for suspicious activity, the platform does real-time traversals to uncover all connected signals across the graph. This allows security systems to identify and disable entire coordinated fraud rings quickly rather than handling individual accounts sequentially.

Here’s how it works. The following query uses full-text keyword search and vector similarity search to traverse connected entities across multiple hops to identify a target entity linked to known suspicious activity. Note that the query is illustrative and the field names have been anonymized.

Recent findings suggest that today, the graph-based abuse detection platform operates as a unified, Google-wide defense platform across a live graph of over 500 billion nodes and 1 trillion edges. Further, bringing ability to do multi-hop graph queries to real-time enforcement has fundamentally changed how Google stops abuse, delivering massive wins for customers and end users:.

Safeguarding advertiser budgets: The graph-based abuse detection platform is a primary source of detection signals for ad policy enforcement across Google's ad products. By uncovering the coordinated networks behind click fraud, click farms, and invalid traffic in real time, it stops bad actors, so advertisers don’t waste budget on invalid interactions.

Defending users against emerging threats: Real-time relationship analysis helps Google catch public-figure impersonation, account takeovers, cloaking, and landing-page malware before campaigns start to scale. During any incident, the graph-based abuse detection platform plays a vital role in tracing the connected assets and rapidly shutting down the attack.

Stopping repeat financial offenders: By correlating billing, financial, and identity information the platform identifies repeat bad actors and prevents banned offenders from simply spinning up upcoming accounts to evade enforcement.

Google's graph-based abuse detection platform for ads shows what Spanner Graph can deliver under the world’s most demanding scale and latency requirements. Because this unified relational and graph architecture is built directly into Spanner, enterprises across a variety of industries can use the same foundation to solve their own complex pattern-matching and fraud challenges:.

Industry observers note that retail and e-commerce: Retailers connect customer accounts, payments, and shipping data to stop promo abuse and bot networks at checkout. For instance, Target rebuilt its Gift Finder using Spanner Graph and vector search (GraphRAG), cutting maintenance by 50% with sub-10ms latency. Additionally, PayPal uses Spanner Graph for its Customer Graph to unify customer identities across brands.

It has been revealed that cybersecurity and threat intelligence: Security teams map network assets, login origins, and access permissions to uncover attack paths and isolate compromised infrastructure during live incidents. Unifying graph queries with relational telemetry in Spanner helps expose proxy networks and automated impersonators before lateral movement occurs.

According to recent reports, financial services and payments: Risk teams correlate billing data and payment instruments to stop synthetic identity rings and fraud. Equifax uses Spanner Graph to map ownership hierarchies across 30 million businesses.

The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • The first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern prepares the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

Sources indicate that A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub complications made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt indicates: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

In a recent development, at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

Sources indicate that A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

In a recent development, on the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

According to recent reports, the agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Recent findings suggest that training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

Industry observers note that no dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

In a recent development, paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

Sources indicate that if you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • OpenSearch Memory stores the original events verbatim, makes them searchable within seconds, and asynchronously derives structured memories.
  • Amazon OpenSearch Memory is available today in US East (N.

Today, AWS declared the general availability of Amazon OpenSearch Memory, a new serverless capability in Amazon OpenSearch Service for adding persistent memory to AI agents. OpenSearch Memory stores agent interactions as searchable events, derives useful memories, and retrieves relevant context across sessions, so agents can recall prior decisions, earlier interactions, and user preferences without replaying the full conversation history to the model. Customers can give agents long-term memory without provisioning infrastructure or building separate extraction, indexing, consolidation, and retrieval systems.

OpenSearch Memory stores the original events verbatim, makes them searchable within seconds, and asynchronously derives structured memories. It manages the full memory lifecycle, including extraction, embedding, indexing, consolidation (adding, updating, or skipping memories as new information arrives), and retrieval using keyword, semantic, and hybrid search. Customers control access with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) for each memory store, with actor and session scoping, and can set expiration periods for events and memories. Because it is serverless, there are no clusters to provision, instance types to choose, or indexes to create, and capacity for extraction and search scales automatically.

Amazon OpenSearch Memory is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) Regions. For pricing details about Amazon OpenSearch Memory, visit the pricing page.

Industry observers note that to learn more about Amazon OpenSearch Memory, see the technical documentation and launch blog. You can get started by visiting the technical launch blog that details how to add persistent memory to your agents with Amazon OpenSearch Memory.

arXiv:2611.24302v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

As organizations move from reactive analytics to proactive systems of action powered by autonomous AI agents, data platforms face a new set of demands. Moving from human scale to agent scale changes both how data pipelines run and how they are built: Teams and AI agents now use Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and agentic troubleshooting to build, submit, and diagnose Apache Spark pipelines while preparing multimodal datasets, performing feature engineering, and acting on live business signals around the clock. Over the past year, customer use of Managed Service for Apache Spark in serverless deployments has nearly doubled, with millions of jobs running each month as enterprises build on Google’s Agentic Data Cloud.

It has been revealed that in the Agentic Data Cloud, Apache Spark doesn't operate in isolation. Managed Service for Apache Spark runs on Google Cloud's borderless lakehouse, so Apache Spark and BigQuery can read and write the same tables with high performance. Through Knowledge Catalog, both engines share centralized governance, consistent policies, detailed lineage, and semantic discovery for AI agents.

It has been revealed that today, we are announcing the general availability of Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, debuting a next-generation runtime foundation for serverless and managed cluster deployments. Engineered to power both modern enterprise data pipelines and fast-growing agentic workloads, Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 introduces:.

A latest 4.0 runtime with Apache Spark 4.2: Standardized on Apache Spark 4.2, Java 25, Python 3.13 with Pixi, and Apache Iceberg 1.12, it is now available for both serverless and managed clusters.

A redesigned, code-first Google Cloud console and agentic troubleshooting: Onboard rapidly with a new Overview page featuring a samples gallery, Lakehouse public datasets, and one-click VS Code authoring in Cloud Shell, manage all serverless and cluster workloads from a unified Jobs view, and use an AI agent to automatically diagnose job failures.

Third-party IDE integration with the Data Agent Kit: Configure MCP servers, skills, and API access to build and run Apache Spark pipelines directly from VS Code, Claude Code, and Antigravity.

Faster startups and Lightning Engine acceleration: Run on default Gen4 infrastructure with faster startups at no additional cost, and accelerate workloads with Lightning Engine for up to 3.25x the price-performance over the leading high-speed Apache Spark alternative.

This fresh runtime packages Apache Spark 4.2 (including Spark Declarative Pipelines and Real-Time Mode), Java 25, Scala 2.13, Apache Iceberg 1.12, Delta Lake 4.4, and Python 3.13 with Pixi for faster dependency management.

It has been revealed that managed Spark serverless and cluster workloads now run on the same modern stack whether written by a data engineer or generated by data engineering and data science skills in Gemini, Claude, and other large language models (LLMs). Teams can standardize on one set of component versions and move PySpark, Scala, and Spark SQL workloads between serverless and managed clusters.

Data teams should spend their time writing Spark logic rather than configuring infrastructure, hunting for the right job, or digging through driver and executor logs when something fails. Version 4.0 ships alongside a redesigned, code-first Google Cloud console built to take that operational work off their plate.

The refreshed console streamlines every stage of the Apache Spark lifecycle:.

Frictionless onboarding and one-click authoring: A redesigned Overview page helps developers get started immediately with an integrated samples gallery, pre-loaded Lakehouse public datasets, guided demos, and one-click authoring in VS Code through Cloud Shell.

It has been revealed that optimized defaults and reusable runtime profiles: Out-of-the-box performance defaults simplify job submission and cluster creation. With reusable runtime profiles (in preview) for batch and interactive workloads, platform admins can capture governed hardware, network, and autoscaling baselines once so developers can simply select a profile and run code.

Unified job, session, and fleet management: Engineers can submit and monitor batch jobs, interactive serverless sessions, and managed clusters from a single unified listing, backed by streamlined fleet management and redesigned detail views that surface key performance metrics and logs in one place.

Agentic troubleshooting: When a job fails or slows down, an AI agent analyzes logs, metrics, and query plans within existing IAM permissions to identify the likely root cause and recommend a fix, helping engineers swiftly return a failed job to a healthy state.

Image 1: Gemini Cloud Assist investigates a failed Apache Spark job, forms a hypothesis, and points to the likely root cause without leaving the job page.

Image 2: One Jobs page for every Apache Spark workload across serverless and managed clusters, with tier and runtime version at a glance.

According to recent reports, many data engineers and data scientists would rather never leave their editor. With the Data Agent Kit, they can build and run Apache Spark workloads from VS Code, Antigravity, Claude Code, and other agentic IDEs. Setup takes a few clicks: pick Apache Spark and the other services you use, and the kit configures Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agent skills, and API access for each one. From there, AI agents can generate, tune, and test Apache Spark pipelines on Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 without leaving the IDE.

Image 3: In VS Code, the Data Agent Kit sets up MCP servers, skills, and API access for Apache Spark and other services.

As practitioners and AI agents trigger short-running, ephemeral jobs on demand to prepare data, perform feature engineering, and answer ad-hoc queries, low startup latency and predictable price-performance are essential to avoiding a cost spiral. In Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, our performance-optimized serverless experience removes manual infrastructure tuning through three changes:.

Faster startups at no additional cost: On the serverless Premium tier, runtime and control-plane optimizations in version 4.0 deliver faster startup times than previous runtime versions across interactive sessions and short-running batch workloads at no additional cost.

In a recent development, hardware acceleration by default: Upcoming serverless 4.0 workloads run on the Premium tier by default, using Google Cloud's latest-generation Gen4 VM instances and Hyperdisk storage. Teams get our highest-efficiency compute and storage fleet without picking machine types or configuring disks, while aligning infrastructure tiering directly with workload urgency.

Software acceleration with Lightning Engine: Our native C++ vectorized execution engine, Lightning Engine, is available in the 4.0 runtime and delivers up to 3.25x the price-performance over the leading high-speed Apache Spark alternative, along with up to 4.9x faster performance compared to running open-source Apache Spark with zero code changes. Built on Apache Gluten and Velox with Google-specific optimizations, Lightning Engine compiles Apache Spark DataFrame, Dataset, and Spark SQL query plans into native SIMD instructions. For lakehouse storage, built-in intelligent caching accelerates file scan times on Apache Iceberg tables by up to 50%. Separately, for workloads querying BigQuery, Lightning Engine's native reader uses Apache Arrow streams to accelerate BigQuery reads by up to 40% compared to default BigQuery reads in Managed Service for Apache Spark. In the 4.0 runtime, Lightning Engine expands support to ARM processors, Ubuntu images, and native vectorized readers for Apache ORC and CSV alongside Apache Parquet, Apache Iceberg, and Delta Lake.

"We were facing not only processing challenges, we were facing management overhead across thousands of servers in our ecosystem, so we migrated to serverless Managed Service for Apache Spark. We moved from managing infrastructure to a no-ops infrastructure. Not only did it help us overcome maintenance and cluster management challenges, it helped us optimize our costs at scale to meet our business SLAs. Apache Spark is no longer just compute for us; it is a strategic business accelerator."—Saurabh Kumar, Senior Director of Data Engineering, Lowe's.

In a recent development, when autonomous agents and production pipelines run around the clock, tying a workload to a single machine shape or zone can stall downstream decisions when regional demand spikes. Without dedicated reservations, cloud service providers may not always have available capacity during peak demand. We are introducing infrastructure fungibility for serverless deployments to improve resource availability for all customers:.

Serverless infrastructure fungibility and fallback: Serverless 4.0 workloads are no longer tied to one VM instance family, disk type, or zone. The platform selects from several latest-generation VM instance families and disk types across zones in the region. If the preferred infrastructure is constrained during a local demand peak, the service automatically chooses the best available infrastructure in the same region instead of failing the job. Once capacity returns, workloads go back to the default Gen4 VM instances and Hyperdisk infrastructure.

Data Compute Unit (DCU) quotas: Quotas for serverless deployments are now set in DCUs rather than per machine family. Because the platform selects the VM instance family, admins manage one unified DCU quota instead of separate CPU quotas for each machine type.

A borderless lakehouse breaks down walled gardens by connecting operational, analytical, and cross-cloud data in open formats without moving it. In Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, Apache Iceberg ships directly in the runtime image, and every workload automatically has access to the serverless Lakehouse runtime catalog. Teams no longer have to configure a lakehouse metastore with Apache Spark or complete prerequisites such as setting up Google Cloud Storage (GCS) directories beforehand, so they can focus straight on writing business logic. Version 4.0 also eliminates the need for GCS staging buckets and uses end-user credentials by default.

Through the Lakehouse runtime catalog, Managed Service for Apache Spark, BigQuery, and AlloyDB can directly read and write the same Apache Iceberg tables on GCS without ETL pipelines or data copies. Everything registered in the Lakehouse runtime catalog automatically surfaces in Knowledge Catalog, which enriches metadata and business context so AI agents and Gemini can query and reason over tables curated with Apache Spark with high accuracy, governed access controls, and lower token costs.

To see how these capabilities come together across end-to-end architectures, read our Google Cloud Apache Spark in the Agentic Era whitepaper. The whitepaper walks through practical design patterns for multimodal data preparation, large-scale feature engineering, and connecting AI agents to governed Apache Iceberg tables through MCP tools and Knowledge Catalog.

Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 is available for serverless and managed cluster deployments across all Managed Service for Apache Spark regions. The fastest way to try version 4.0 is the Data Agent Kit: install it in VS Code, Claude Code, or Antigravity to build and run Apache Spark workloads on version 4.0 with AI agents right from your IDE. You can also start from the latest Overview page in the Google Cloud console, which walks you from code to a running job.

To learn more, read the Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 documentation for serverless deployments and managed clusters, and try the hands-on Lightning Engine codelab.
