💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Cognito now supports OAuth dynamic client registration (DCR, RFC 7591).
  • It has been revealed that with DCR, Cognito advertises a registration endpoint in its OAuth authorization server metadata.
  • Recent findings suggest that DCR is available on the Essentials and Plus feature plans in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available.

Amazon Cognito now supports OAuth dynamic client registration (DCR, RFC 7591). Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices in minutes. With DCR support, Model Context Protocol (MCP) clients and AI agents can register themselves at runtime. Previously, you had to create an application client in advance for each AI client before it could connect to an MCP server that uses Cognito for authorization.

It has been revealed that with DCR, Cognito advertises a registration endpoint in its OAuth authorization server metadata. MCP clients that support dynamic client registration discover the endpoint, register to receive a client ID, and then sign people in. You control who can register: either require registration requests to present an access token with a registration scope, or turn on open registration so that any client can register. Dynamically registered clients appear with your other app clients with a client ID prefix and a client type you can filter on, so you can manage them with the same console and APIs.

Recent findings suggest that DCR is available on the Essentials and Plus feature plans in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available. To learn more, see Dynamic client registration in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.

Drowning in clicks: Scaling Black Friday pipelines with Managed Airflow agents

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2323 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Product Manager, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.
  • Software Engineer, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.
  • When an Airflow pipeline fails in production, the hard part is rarely the fix.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sr. Product Manager, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.

Software Engineer, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

When an Airflow pipeline fails in production, the hard part is rarely the fix. It's finding out what to fix. A task dies without a traceback. Is it the code, the data, or the environment? Hard to say, as clues are scattered across task logs, scheduler logs, and worker metrics. And once you know what the problem is, the question becomes whether to add memory, rewrite the DAG, or finally take on the major version upgrade you've been putting off. Answering these questions takes time and deep Airflow expertise, usually while you're on call in the middle of an incident.

According to recent reports, AI agents can increasingly do much of this legwork. Managed Service for Apache Airflow (formerly Cloud Composer) now offers agentic help across a pipeline's entire lifecycle. In the Google Cloud console, Managed Airflow Agent investigates failed tasks, recommends improvements to your environment, and checks whether your DAGs are ready for a newer Airflow version. In your IDE or coding agent, Data Agent Kit writes, migrates, and deploys DAGs. In this post, we take you on a tour of these features through a story of a fictional manufacturer, Cymbal Shops.

According to recent reports, amira is a data engineer at Cymbal Shops, an online retailer running cymbal-prod, a production Managed Airflow (Gen 3) environment whose workers have 2 vCPUs, 4 GB of memory, and that autoscale between 1 and 6. Every click, search, and add-to-cart on Cymbal's website and mobile app goes to a Pub/Sub topic. A Cloud Storage subscription writes the events as newline-delimited JSON files into hourly folders under gs://cymbal-clickstream-landing/events/. It writes files in parallel and starts fresh ones every 5 minutes or every 128 MB, whichever comes first.

Analysts, meanwhile, want these events in BigQuery, cleaned and with personal data hashed — and they want them fast. Ideally, each file would be processed the moment it lands. But Cymbal's Airflow environment runs Airflow 2.11.1, and Airflow 2 has no native way to start a DAG run when something happens outside Airflow. You can get close: Schedule a DAG every few minutes and let a sensor wait for latest files, or build an extra service that triggers runs through the Airflow REST API. However, the team doesn't want all those moving parts, so they settle for the next best thing: an hourly batch.

Amira writes her DAGs with an agent. She works in Antigravity with the Data Agent Kit plugin, which adds Google Data Cloud skills and tools to the agent, and she uses Gemini as her model. Setup takes a few minutes: She installs the plugin, signs in with her Google account, and selects her project and region.

In the agent panel, she describes what she needs with this prompt:.

"Write a DAG named clickstream_hourly for the Managed Airflow environment cymbal-prod in us-central1. Every hour, load the previous hour of clickstream events into the BigQuery table clickstream.events. The events are newline-delimited JSON files in gs://cymbal-clickstream-landing/events/YYYY-MM-DD/HH/. Transform them with pandas: read each file into a DataFrame with the nested context object kept as a JSON string, combine the files with pd.concat, then drop malformed records, deduplicate on event_id (Pub/Sub delivers at least once), and hash user_email and ip_address. Re-running an hour must not create duplicates. If a run fails, email data-oncall@example.com. Validate the DAG and deploy it.".

Data Agent Kit inspects the target Managed Airflow environment in Antigravity, generates an Airflow 2.11-compatible DAG, and deploys it.

Sources indicate that the agent checks the target environment before it writes any code. Because cymbal-prod runs Airflow 2.11.1, the agent produces the code aligned to that version. It then deploys the DAG to cymbal-prod and confirms that Airflow loads it without errors.

It has been revealed that amira reviews the code, and the DAG goes live in early August. It's good code: readable, idempotent, and correct for Airflow 2.11. A busy hour sees about 200 files and 350 MB, and the task peaks below 2 GB — well under the 4 GB worker limit.

Look at how the task builds its input, though. It lists every file in the hour's folder, reads each one into a DataFrame, and then pd.concat combines them into a single DataFrame. The unit of work is a clock hour, so the task needs more memory as traffic grows. That's fine until traffic changes...

The hourly task loads every JSON file from the previous hour into memory and combines them into a single DataFrame with pd.concat.

Industry observers note that late October brings two changes in the same week. Cymbal launches its "Fall Into Savings" campaign, and a newly introduced mobile app release adds much more detailed event tracking. Events from the new app version are about three times larger than their predecessors, and the campaign brings more traffic on top, so an hour of clicks grows from about 350 MB to about 1.4 GB. Holding a whole hour in pandas takes several times its raw size, so load_previous_hour_clickstream now needs more memory than a worker’s allotted 4 GB. Autoscaling doesn't help here: It adds workers when tasks queue up, but each task still runs on a single worker and can't use more memory than that worker has.

On October 23, the 14:00 UTC run of clickstream_hourly fails. All three attempts die the same way, with no error in the task log.

Amira opens cymbal-prod in the console, where Managed Airflow Agent is built in. It diagnoses the problem and recommends a fix; Amira decides what to change.

Industry observers note that she goes to the DAGs tab, selects clickstream_hourly, and opens Run history. Next to the failed 14:00 run there's an Investigate button with a sparkle icon. She clicks it, and a short ‘Investigate DAG run failure’ dialog asks her to confirm her choice. The Ask agent panel then opens next to the page, and the agent starts investigating.

Managed Airflow Agent investigates the failed run in the console, correlates worker memory metrics with task retries, and recommends fixes.

At the end of the report, the agent recommends three fixes: load the files straight into BigQuery, process them in batches, or give the workers more memory.

Look at what the agent delivers! Every conclusion includes the evidence that led to it, so Amira can check the reasoning herself.

It has been revealed that two of the recommendations are code changes, and code changes take time to write and test. With every hourly run now failing, Amira needs the quick fix first: more memory for the workers. But how much? The right number depends on the whole environment, not on one task. So she asks the agent in the same panel:.

It has been revealed that "clickstream_hourly runs out of memory on 4 GB workers. Analyze the cymbal-prod environment and recommend how much worker memory it needs, along with any other improvements.".

Managed Airflow Agent analyzes environment-wide telemetry, recommends 8 GB worker memory, and flags resilience and retention gaps.

The agent recommends increasing worker memory from 4 GB to 8 GB, and flags three production-readiness gaps: Database retention is disabled, the environment isn't highly resilient, and it has no scheduled snapshots.

Amira acts on the first recommendation right away. The agent is read-only, so she makes the change herself and increases worker memory to 8 GB.

She schedules the other two recommendations for the next change window. With 8 GB workers, the pipeline gets through the rest of the campaign.

But that only buys time. Black Friday traffic is forecast at 8 to 10 times a normal peak hour, and at that volume the hourly batch will need well over 8 GB. The troubleshooting report had already named the real problem: a unit of work that grows with traffic. That brings Amira back to what the team wanted in the first place, which was to process each file as soon as it lands.

In a recent development, airflow 3 makes that much easier, because it supports event-driven scheduling natively. An asset watcher listens to an external source, such as a Pub/Sub subscription. When upcoming messages arrive, it updates an asset, and any DAG scheduled on that asset starts a run. Under the hood, the watcher still checks the subscription every few seconds, but it does so inside Airflow's triggerer. No DAG needs to be scheduled just so a sensor can wait for files, and no extra service has to trigger runs. Each run gets the new messages in its payload, so it can work on just the files that landed, one task per file, and memory per task depends on file size, not on how busy the hour is.

Recent findings suggest that A major version upgrade of a production environment isn't something to do blind. Before anyone touches the code, Amira asks the agent in the same panel:.

"Check whether cymbal-prod is ready to upgrade to Airflow 3.".

Managed Airflow Agent can also check upgrade readiness. It checks compatibility of the environment's DAGs with a given version. Amira is checking what problems she might have while migrating to Airflow 3.3.1 (composer-3-airflow-3.3.1-build.3). The agent reports the following observations:.

Managed Airflow Agent scans DAGs in cymbal-prod for Airflow 3 compatibility blockers before migration.

It has been revealed that two findings are blockers. The first comes as a surprise: a maintenance DAG that cleans up the Airflow database by hand, which Airflow 3 no longer allows. The agent's fix is to retire it and turn on database retention, the same feature it recommended during the incident. The second, marketing_attribution, still uses execution_date, which Airflow 3 removed. Four DAGs also need schedule_interval renamed to schedule.

In a few minutes, the agent estimated the work to be done. To perform the upgrade, the report suggests using Data Agent Kit's migrations skill.

Rather than upgrading in place, Amira creates a fresh Airflow 3 environment alongside cymbal-prod to move the DAGs there.

It has been revealed that back in Antigravity, Data Agent Kit's migrations skill takes over. It adapts existing DAGs to the target Airflow version, deploys them, and verifies them. Finally, the agent deploys the DAGs to cymbal-prod-af3 and confirms that they load without errors.

Data Agent Kit's migrations skill refactors the pipeline to Airflow 3 event-driven scheduling and verifies deployment in cymbal-prod-af3.

Two design choices remove the original problem:.

Scheduling moves into the watcher. PubsubPullTrigger is an event trigger, so an AssetWatcher can use it directly. The triggerer checks the subscription every 10 seconds in the background. Each batch of messages becomes an asset event that starts a run, with the messages in its payload. Nothing waits for the top of the hour, and no extra service has to call the Airflow REST API.

Each task processes one file rather than a full hour. Dynamic task mapping gives each new file its own task, and the subscription caps files at 128 MB. A busier hour means more tasks, not bigger ones.

Once the upcoming DAG proves itself on live traffic, Amira pauses the hourly DAG in cymbal-prod.

Success! In a load test that replayed eight times normal peak traffic, clickstream_ingest simply ran more often. Memory per task didn't change.

Before: Airflow 2, hourly batch.

One clock hour: about 350 MB normally, 1.4 GB at campaign peak.

One file, a few MB each (at most 128 MB).

Grows with traffic: about 5 to 6 GB at campaign peak, well over 8 GB forecast for Black Friday.

Industry observers note that each agent works from the right vantage point. The console agent inspects production telemetry with your permissions and doesn't change anything, while the coding agent works in the IDE where code changes get reviewed, tested, and deployed.

Each step sets up the next one. The troubleshooting report offered a wider review, and each recommendation came with actionable advice. The upgrade check ended with next steps for the migrations skill, turning its report into the brief for the migration.

Agents propose and people decide. Amira scaled the workers, ran the infrastructure commands, and reviewed every change.

In a recent development, static inspection estimates the work before live migration. Checking compatibility in the console scoped the effort in minutes, and the migration agent then made and verified the changes in a real environment.

Industry observers note that amira used the agents built into the console and her IDE. Two other capabilities didn't fit her story but are worth knowing about:.

You can bring your own agent with the Managed Airflow MCP server, now generally available, so any MCP-compatible agent can manage your environments, allowing you to list and trigger DAGs, check run status, and inspect failed task instances. Access is controlled through IAM, and read-only tools are flagged so you can limit agents to them.

Run agentic steps inside your pipelines with the Apache Airflow Common AI provider, which adds model-driven tasks that run side by side with deterministic ones in the same Airflow 3 DAG. Examples include LLM-based branching, agentic retries that tell a transient error from a bad input, and schema drift detection.

Explore Managed Airflow Agent troubleshooting and the overview of agentic capabilities.

Install Google Cloud Data Agent Kit using the documentation, the extension for VS Code, the plugin for coding agents (Antigravity, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Codex CLI), or the open-source Airflow agent skills.

Learn about Airflow 3 event-driven scheduling.

Connect your agents to the Managed Airflow MCP server.

Build model-driven tasks and agents in DAGs with the Apache Airflow Common AI provider.

Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (232 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.24075v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. We find that this difficulty has an important geometric structure. Under an operating-condition shift, the embedding space of a TSFM does not move uniformly: some local regions change substantially, while others remain nearly unchanged. Consequently, a global adaptation can unnecessarily move embeddings that were already correctly classified. To address this, we propose the novel PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport). PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for the regions affected by each new condition. An explicit identity path is always retained, and a learned gate softly selects among the identity and accumulated transports for each input. The pretrained TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports remain fixed. With only 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition and no condition identity at test time, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream. Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/PACT.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AWS Network Load Balancer (NLB) now supports mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication for clients that present X.509 certificates.
  • According to recent reports, mutual TLS is commonly used to secure communication between IoT devices, APIs, and microservices, and in regulated environments where both sides must prove their identity.
  • Mutual TLS for NLB is available in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions where NLB is available.

In a recent development, AWS Network Load Balancer (NLB) now supports mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication for clients that present X.509 certificates. Until now, customers who needed mTLS with NLB built their own solutions or ran third-party proxies to authenticate clients. With this launch, NLB verifies client certificates on its TLS listeners, so only trusted clients can reach your targets. You can offload the compute-intensive processing required for mTLS authentication to NLB, without adding certificate logic to your backend applications.

According to recent reports, mutual TLS is commonly used to secure communication between IoT devices, APIs, and microservices, and in regulated environments where both sides must prove their identity. To use mTLS, create a trust store with a certificate authority (CA) certificate bundle from a CA of your choice or AWS Private Certificate Authority, and attach it to a newly introduced or existing NLB TLS listener. To block certificates you no longer trust, add one or more certificate revocation lists (CRLs) to the trust store. To admit only specific clients, add client certificate filters that match the Common Name, Organizational Unit, or the DNS name or URI in the Subject Alternative Name, such as a SPIFFE ID. You can set up mTLS with the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or APIs.

Mutual TLS for NLB is available in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions where NLB is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Blog and the NLB User Guide.

  • It has been revealed that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

It has been revealed that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

In a recent development, overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All upcoming data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Recent findings suggest that alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

Recent findings suggest that the multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

According to recent reports, while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the upcoming release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Recent findings suggest that apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

In a recent development, structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

Industry observers note that all recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

Sources indicate that the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

According to recent reports, proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been revealed by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

In a recent development, thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team declared the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

Recent findings suggest that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

Recent findings suggest that if you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

arXiv:2611.24073v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. Evaluation spans (1) objective code-level functional acceptance against the game specification, (2) agent-based QA and playtesting of 3D presentation and playability, and (3) blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena. The preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved, and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference. The public arena is hosted online.

Attention Is Not Relevance: Challenging the Causality of Attention in Autonomous Driving

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (253 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.24051v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Attention has become one of the most widely adopted solutions for estimating the relevance of surrounding objects and interpreting an autonomous vehicle's driving decisions. However, its ability to capture the causal impact of individual input elements on an AI model's output has long been discussed in the literature, particularly in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) domain. This work brings this discussion into the autonomous driving domain by analyzing the accuracy of attention in estimating the impact of an input object on an autonomous vehicle's driving, i.e., its relevance. To this end, we compare different attention-based relevance estimation methods against a causal reference of object relevance obtained through counterfactual analysis. We perform our analysis on more than 80,000 synthetic driving scenes using an autonomous vehicle based on PlanT 2.0, a state-of-the-art Transformer-based model for object-level planning. Results show that attention provides a correlational rather than causal indication of object relevance. Attention-based relevance estimation methods do not consistently identify all relevant objects and tend to incorrectly classify as relevant objects with little or no impact on the vehicle's driving. In particular, results show that attention can effectively identify relevant objects in simple single-lane, straight-road scenarios, but its accuracy degrades in more complex settings, such as multi-lane roads and intersections. These findings highlight the limitations of attention as a proxy for object relevance, calling for novel methods able to accurately capture the causal impact of individual objects on the vehicle's driving and distinguish it from correlational associations.

Industry observers note that AWS Partner Central introduced the BVR motion on June 16, 2026, to help Partners drive business outcomes for their customers by structuring AWS service adoption into defined stages, with funding tied to demonstrated value. Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.24039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic AI platforms-systems in which LLM agents plan, invoke tools, retain memory and coordinate to change the state of enterprise systems-are being procured faster than they can be measured. Public agent benchmarks score models in fixed harnesses; enterprises buy integrated platforms whose orchestration, memory, governance and tooling layers dominate outcomes, and they buy them largely on the strength of vendor demonstrations. We report an industrial evaluation programme ("bakeoff") run by the innovation laboratory of a global bank in which ten platforms-spanning open-source frameworks, proprietary products and hyperscaler ecosystems-were assessed by a cross-functional panel on nine capability dimensions across three financial-services workloads: counterparty credit risk, retrieval-augmented generation and process automation. Scores separate the field into three tiers that are stable under alternative weightings, and surface workload-specific strengths that aggregates hide. A secondary analysis, however, finds Cronbach's alpha = 0.98 across nominally distinct dimensions and rank correlations >= 0.93 with the total for eight of nine: a halo effect indicating that demonstration-based scoring measures presentation as much as capability. From these lessons we propose a gate-then-score evaluation protocol with four layers (capability, execution reliability, governance gates, business value), trace-level reliability metrics estimated over repeated runs, an autonomy-readiness scale and a reproducibility protocol. We state precisely what the present evidence supports, and what a controlled harness must add to turn enterprise platform evaluation from structured judgement into measurement.

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Sources indicate that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • According to recent reports, beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Sources indicate that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

According to recent reports, beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

According to recent reports, reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

Recent findings suggest that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Industry observers note that beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

It has been revealed that attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

It has been revealed that the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

In a recent development, the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

In a recent development, only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Sources indicate that beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

It has been revealed that every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

Industry observers note that the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

Recent findings suggest that A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

Recent findings suggest that the pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel initiative. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

According to recent reports, we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

In a recent development, below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

According to recent reports, † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Industry observers note that don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

Sources indicate that the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

According to recent reports, after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Recent findings suggest that training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

In a recent development, sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

According to recent reports, update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one enhancement behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Recent findings suggest that you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Recent findings suggest that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

Sources indicate that we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

Industry observers note that for the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot indicates the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

In a recent development, decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

In a recent development, we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

It has been revealed that first, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

It has been revealed that for a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

Sources indicate that that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

Ultimate guide for fixing your team’s API keys

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most Gemini prototypes start the same way.
  • It has been revealed that the trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real people and the key comes along unchanged.
  • For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype. That speed is the point, and shouldn’t be slowed down.

It has been revealed that the trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real people and the key comes along unchanged. By then it usually isn't one key. Every developer has their own, often several, sitting in .env files, shell profiles and chat threads. The app has one more, baked into its config.

For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month. One of those keys ends up in a public repo, a Slack channel or a mobile app bundle. Automated scrapers find it within minutes and use it to run large workloads. By the time the first billing alert arrives, the bill is in the tens of thousands. Under the shared responsibility model, the customer pays for usage made with their own valid credentials. For a seed-stage organization, that’s runway gone in a weekend.

In our recent post, 10 questions every startup should answer before moving to production with their AI prototype, we covered the whole path from prototype to production. This post goes deeper on one part of it: getting off raw API keys entirely.

Here is what this guide covers:.

It has been revealed that authorize your people. Give everyone on the team one login with Application Default Credentials and use it to call Gemini, Claude and open models. Steps 1 and 2 take about five minutes.

Authorize your application. Run your app under its own service account with only the access it needs. Steps 3 and 4.

According to recent reports, lock down what's left. Move the remaining keys into Secret Manager, then add spend caps, guardrails and monitoring. Step 5 and the closing sections.

The code for every step is in a companion repo with runnable samples and offline tests.

An AI Studio key is a bearer token. Whoever holds it can use it. It doesn't expire on its own. It isn't tied to a machine, a person or a workload. It has no spending limit unless you add one. When someone leaves the tech giant, nobody knows which keys to revoke.

Recent findings suggest that that is fine on your laptop while you are the only user. It stops being fine when any of these is true:.

A key has left your laptop. It was shared in chat, committed to a repo or deployed to a server.

More than one person on the team needs to call the API.

You are spending more than a few hundred dollars a month, or you are about to onboard paying customers.

If one of those describes you, do the switch this week.

In a recent development, before changing anything, find out where your keys are. The repo includes a small scanner that looks for strings shaped like Google API keys and for api_key= set to a literal value. It reports the file and line but never the key itself. It also exits with an error, so you can drop it into CI:.

Each person on the team runs one command:.

According to recent reports, A browser window opens, you sign in with your work account and gcloud stores a short-lived credential on your machine. Every Google Cloud SDK finds it automatically. There is no key to copy, paste or leak.

Then point your tools at the team project:.

Sources indicate that someone has to grant you access to the project first. Step four shows how.

That single credential works for every model in Model Garden, not only Gemini. You don't need fresh accounts, new keys or separate invoices. Within each SDK, switching models means changing one string.

Gemini, with the Google Gen AI SDK. If your prototype builds the client with api_key=..., this is the only change:.

According to recent reports, enterprise=True sends the call to Gemini Platform instead of AI Studio. Older samples call the same flag vertexai=True, and current SDK versions accept both.

Claude, with Anthropic's SDK and the same login:.

Open models such as OpenAI's gpt-oss, with the OpenAI SDK pointed at Google Cloud:.

Partner models like Claude need a one-time Enable on their Model Garden card in each project. After that, everyone with access can call them.

Sources indicate that openAI's GPT-6 models arrived in Model Garden on October 21 in private preview for select enterprise customers. When they open up, the same login will work for them too.

Every call lands on one Google Cloud bill, which makes it easier to compare models on cost and quality.

Industry observers note that your app needs the same thing your developers just got: an identity instead of a key. For a workload, that identity is a service account.

According to recent reports, the good news is that the code from Step 2 doesn't change. On your laptop, ADC picks up your own login. On Cloud Run, GKE or Compute Engine, it picks up a short-lived token for the service account attached to the workload, refreshed automatically. So there is nothing in your codebase to leak. A token that escapes is short-lived, usually about an hour, and it only carries the permissions of one service account.

Create the service account and deploy with it:.

Keep people and production apart. Developers work in my-startup-dev under their own logins, and the app runs in my-startup-prod under its service account. A mistake in one doesn't spend the other's budget.

Removing keys solves the leak problem. The next question is what each identity is allowed to do. If a person or a service account holds the Editor or Owner role, a stolen login or token can still delete resources, change permissions or read data it never needed.

Calling models takes one role, roles/aiplatform.user. The grant looks the same for both kinds of identity.

For people, grant it to a Google group, not to individuals. Onboarding and offboarding then become a group membership change:.

For the app, grant it to the service account:.

According to recent reports, it takes about 30 seconds longer than granting Editor. If anything is compromised later, the attacker gets one narrow role instead of the whole project. When someone leaves, remove them from the group and their access ends everywhere at once.

In a recent development, in the Cloud Console, the Grant access dialog has a Help me choose roles button. You describe the task in plain English and Gemini suggests predefined roles. By default the suggestions cover common tasks, which usually means a service's broad Admin, Editor or Viewer role. To get the narrow roles, say so:.

What is the narrowest access a service account needs to call Gemini models on Agent Platform?

Three more controls are worth knowing:.

Sources indicate that if your project sits in an organization, the vertexai.allowedModels policy limits which models anyone can call. You list values such as publishers/google/models/gemini-4-hydrogen:predict, and everything else is blocked.

It has been revealed that the repo includes a one-line audit that lists every service account holding Owner or Editor on a project. Run it now and again before each launch.

To stop fresh keys from being created, enforce Org Policies denying CREATE on apikeys.googleapis.com/Key for API keys and iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation for service account keys.

Some keys won't go away, like Stripe, Slack or your email provider. They belong in Secret Manager, not in .env files, chat threads or the repo. Access works the way it did in Step 4: grant read access on each secret to the identity that needs it.

Test keys go to the developer group:.

Anyone in the group can then fetch the key with their own login:.

Industry observers note that live keys stay in the production project, readable only by the app's service account. The app reads them at startup:.

Reading --data-file=- from standard input keeps the value out of your shell history. Every read is tied to a named person or service account, and rotating a key means adding one fresh version. Nothing is redeployed and no file is copied between laptops.

Recent findings suggest that then finish the job. Go to the AI Studio API keys page and delete every key, personal or shared, that ever left a laptop. A key you have moved away from is still live until you delete it.

In a recent development, once your people and your app run on identities in a Google Cloud project, several protections become available that a bare key can't offer. You don't need all of them on day one. They are worth knowing about before your first launch.

Standard budget alerts send email while the bill keeps climbing. A spend cap budget, currently in Preview, does more. When estimated spend for one service in one project passes the amount you set, new requests to that service are paused until you lift the cap or the next month starts. Alerts go to billing admins and project owners at 50%, 80% and 100%.

You can create one in the console under Budgets & alerts by choosing Spend cap enforcement, or through the Budget API. The repo wraps the API call and has a dry-run flag so you can inspect the request first:.

In a recent development, know the limits before relying on it. Each cap covers a single project and a single service. Agent Platform, the Gemini API, Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions are eligible today. Enforcement runs on estimated cost and is not instant. Any overage is billed as normal, so set the number below the amount you can actually afford to lose. A cap also pauses usage covered by commitments, and after you lift it the service can take up to an hour to recover.

Set one cap on the dev project and another on prod. An experiment then can't drain the budget your customers depend on. For a second layer, lower your Agent Platform quotas to what you really need, so a bug or an agent stuck in a loop runs into a ceiling instead of your card limit.

As soon as real owners can type into your app, someone will try to make it ignore its instructions. Model Armor screens prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, malicious URLs and sensitive data. You create a template once, check each prompt against it and only call the model when it comes back clean. The repo has both halves.

According to recent reports, if your product lets the model write and run code, for example to analyze a customer's spreadsheet, that code should not run inside your application process. With code execution, the model runs Python in a Google-managed sandbox and hands back the result:.

The generated code never sees your environment variables, your files or your database.

Security Command Center surfaces threats and misconfigurations across the project, such as a service account suddenly calling an API it has never used or a workload contacting an unfamiliar host. Together with Cloud Audit Logs, which record who changed what and when, it also gives you the answers your first enterprise customer's security review will ask for. Because every call now comes from a named person or service account, those logs mean something.

Everyone runs gcloud auth application-default login.

Grant roles/aiplatform.user to one Google group, and enable the partner models you want.

Move shared test keys into Secret Manager, readable by the group.

Deploy with a service account that holds roles/aiplatform.user and nothing broader.

Move live third-party keys into Secret Manager, readable only by that service account.

Set a spend cap on each project below the amount you can afford to lose.

For both: Run the key scanner, then delete every AI Studio key at aistudio.google.com/apikey.

None of this slows down building. You keep the speed of the prototype and every model in Model Garden stays one string away. Nobody on the team has to guard a key again. The full code, with a sample for every step and bonus above, is in the companion repo.

Breaking: Test-Time Symmetrization: Scaling Laws for Model-Agnostic Learning under Structure

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (294 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.24032v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Test-time compute has emerged as a powerful way to improve the accuracy of language models at inference time, with scaling laws quantifying how accuracy improves with additional forward passes. Existing scaling laws, however, focus on repeated sampling from a fixed prompt, even though many tasks admit multiple equivalent representations of the same underlying problem. A graph does not depend on how its nodes are numbered, and a program does not depend on the names of its variables, yet language models can change their answers under such rewritings. In this paper, we study test-time symmetrization, which uses forward passes on rewritings of the input and aggregates the resulting answers over the group $G$ of rewritings. We prove that no amount of sampling and repeated decoding from a single representation can replace rewriting, while only $O(\log |G|)$ random rewritings suffice to recover the information provided by all $|G|$ rewritings. The same set of $O(\log |G|)$ rewritings provides simultaneous approximation across models, decoding rules, and sampled reasoning traces, and the logarithmic scaling is optimal in general. We validate the theory with experiments on Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-14B, with chain-of-thought reasoning, on graph reasoning, logical deduction, and multiple-choice question answering. At the same number of forward passes, spending them on rewritings of the input is substantially more accurate than spending them on repeated sampling from the original prompt whenever the model's answer depends on how the input is written, and the number of rewritings needed grows only logarithmically with the number of possible rewritings, as the theory predicts. Our results provide a principled way to enforce symmetries at inference time when they cannot be built into the model, which we call model-agnostic symmetrization.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity adds private certificate authority support

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (222 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity now supports private certificate authorities (CAs) for custom OAuth 2.0 credential providers.
  • Industry observers note that agentCore Identity has supported private IdP connectivity through Amazon VPC Lattice, but until now the IdP still had to present a publicly trusted TLS certificate over that private connection.
  • You can rotate the CA certificate without downtime by combining the current and new certificates in a single PEM file, and remove private CA trust by updating the credential provider without the certificate reference.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity now supports private certificate authorities (CAs) for custom OAuth 2.0 credential providers. If you already connect your agents to identity providers (IdPs) hosted in your VPC, you can now configure those connections to trust certificates issued by your own CA — including AWS Private CA, enterprise CAs, and self-signed root CAs.

Industry observers note that agentCore Identity has supported private IdP connectivity through Amazon VPC Lattice, but until now the IdP still had to present a publicly trusted TLS certificate over that private connection. With private CA support, you store your CA certificate in AWS Secrets Manager or Amazon S3 and reference it from your credential provider configuration. AgentCore Identity uses it to verify the IdP's server certificate directly, removing the need for a publicly trusted certificate or additional infrastructure on the private network path.

You can rotate the CA certificate without downtime by combining the current and new certificates in a single PEM file, and remove private CA trust by updating the credential provider without the certificate reference.

Private CA support for AgentCore Identity is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Identity supports private IdP connectivity. To get started, see Connect to private identity providers in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. To learn more, visit the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore product page.

arXiv:2611.24004v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Spatial reasoning connects visual observations, geometric estimates, and linguistic decisions into a coherent derivation. Yet tool-augmented agents often acquire evidence without clear targets, combine outputs under inconsistent object or reference-frame semantics, and misjudge evidence sufficiency. Thus, more tools or calls do not reliably improve reasoning. We introduce Space-X, a spatial-reasoning framework that self-evolves toward complete, continuous evidence-chain construction. An Execution Agent acquires, associates, and judges evidence per problem using role-specific memory. A Control Agent diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from execution traces and jointly revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory organization, and decision rules. This loop co-evolves capability and evidence use: evidence needs guide capability development; usable results guide actions. Across multiple benchmarks, Space-X yields gains with four base models. Relative to baselines, GPT-6-sol improves answer accuracy on ViewSpatial and MMSI by 50.39% and 23.07%, respectively; Gemini-3.8-Flash gains 47.50% and 25.22% on these benchmarks. This provides a unified route from fragmented spatial clues to traceable, derivable answers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across the 17 deals reported on by FinTech Global this week, there was a total of $991m raised – showcasing a continuous strength in firms securing investment.

This was up on last week, where total of $602m was raised across 14 FinTech deals, a small increase on the previous week where $454.4m was raised across 12 deals.

Two of the top deals this week came from Bulgarian PayTech firm Payhawk and Model ML, a personal AI platform for financial and professional services.

It has been revealed that geographically, the US secured the most deals this week with 8 in total. Trailing in second was Canada with three, whilst Israel, Egypt, Spain, Georgia, the UK and Bulgaria pulled in one.

According to recent reports, market-wise, financial infrastructure firms made up the majority of this week’s deals with four. In joint second were WealthTech and CyberTech firms on three, PayTech, InsurTech and Blockchain firms secured two.

Sources indicate that this week, research from FinTech Global showcased findings of a powerful performance for Global FinTech in this year’s third quarter. The Global FinTech market attracted $27.5bn across 1,275 deals in Q3 2026. Funding climbed 35% from $20.3bn in Q3 2025 but fell 11% from $30.9bn in Q2 2026.

Deal volume fell 2% from 1,306 transactions in Q3 2025 and rose 5% from 1,220 in Q2 2026.

Payhawk raises $280m to build AI-era Finance OS.

According to recent reports, payhawk, the Sofia-founded spend management and finance platform, has closed a $280m Series C round led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. The deal values the organization at $2bn.

The raise takes Payhawk’s total funding past $515m. Every existing backer returned for the round, among them QED, Greenoaks, Lightspeed, Hedosophia and Bek Ventures.

They were joined by first-time investors Galdana Ventures, Cogito Capital, Inveready and Invus, as well as European founders Tomas Okmanas and Didac Lee.

Model ML bags $250m to give every banker an AI agent.

Model ML, a London-based personal AI platform for financial and professional services, has secured $250m in a Series B round that values the company at $1.5bn.

In a recent development, general Atlantic and QED Investors co-led the investment. Evolution Equity Partners, Airtree, Forestay Capital, Y Combinator, FT Partners, Latitude, Inception Fund and 13Books Capital also took part. The deal lifts the total capital raised by Model ML to $350m.

In a recent development, the raise comes after a period of rapid expansion. Over the third quarter of 2026, annual recurring revenue at the firm increased twelvefold compared with the same period a year earlier, while daily active people rose 26-fold.

Blue J lands $176m to put AI agents on tax desks.

Blue J, a tax research and advisory platform, has secured $176m in a Series E round that values the business at above $700m, as it moves beyond answering tax questions to handing the actual workload over to AI agents.

JMI Equity, a growth equity investor, led the raise. Existing backers Oak HC/FT and Sapphire Ventures returned for the round, joined by Intrepid Growth Partners. The valuation also exceeds C$1bn. As part of the deal, JMI Equity principal Jack Duane will take a seat on the Blue J board.

The manufacturer plans to put the capital behind Workflows, its agentic AI product for tax practitioners, and to push further into the United Kingdom and other international markets.

Corma hits $1bn valuation with $125m Series A.

Corma, an AI research lab building foundation models for defensive cybersecurity, has secured $125m in Series A funding at a $1bn valuation, only three months after revealing its seed round.

NEA led the investment, with participation from returning backers Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue. The latest raise takes the company’s total funding to $185m.

Corma’s $60m seed round, led by Sequoia, was revealed in August.

TBC Georgia secures $51m as ADB and IFC back trade finance.

TBC Georgia, a leading Georgian financial institution and member of the London-listed TBC Bank Group, has raised $51m from international commercial banks to widen the availability of trade finance for businesses across Georgia.

The capital comes with guarantee backing from the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC).

Recent findings suggest that it is channelled through two established schemes: the ADB’s Trade and Supply Chain Finance Program and the IFC’s Global Trade Finance Program. Because both institutions stand behind the facility, commercial lenders can extend capital to the Georgian market with added assurance.

Codex lands $30m Series A to scale stablecoin FX.

Codex, a platform that provides foreign exchange infrastructure for stablecoins and fiat currencies, has secured $30m in Series A funding to expand its cross-border payments business.

Industry observers note that pantera headed the investment, which also drew backing from Dragonfly, Coinbase Ventures, Tenet, Reciprocal, Fin Capital, LeadBlock and additional investors. The deal puts the firm’s post-money valuation at $130m.

Both Dragonfly and Coinbase Ventures have backed Codex before, having taken part in its seed round.

Arva AI lands $20m Series A for AI banking agents.

Arva AI, a company that deploys AI agents to make critical banking decisions, has secured $20m in Series A funding as it looks to push its accuracy-focused technology deeper into the bank back office.
